story.hook: My Boss Tried to Charge Me for His Mistake
story.script: My manager called me into his office on a Monday morning and placed a printed invoice on the desk. He said the company had lost a major client because a report went out with the wrong numbers, and he had decided I should reimburse part of the loss because I was the analyst assigned to the account. The amount he wanted from me was more than a month of my salary. I asked which report he meant. He pointed to a file name I recognized immediately. I had prepared the original version on Friday, checked every figure twice, and sent it to him for approval before leaving for the weekend. He told me that did not matter because my name was still in the document properties. I asked whether he had my final email. He said this was not a negotiation and pushed the invoice closer to me. Instead of arguing, I asked him to email the demand so I could keep a copy for payroll. He hesitated, then sent it while I was still sitting there. The message said I had made an unauthorized change to the client's pricing table and that the cost would be deducted from my next two paychecks. I replied with one sentence asking him to confirm that this was the company's final position. He wrote yes. Then I opened the project archive. Our system kept every saved version of client documents, including timestamps and the account used for each edit. My Friday version showed the correct pricing table. At seven forty-three that evening, two hours after I had left the office, my manager had opened the file from home. He changed three percentage values, removed a warning note explaining that the figures were provisional, and saved the document under the same filename. At eight twelve, he emailed that edited version directly to the client without sending it back to me. I downloaded the audit history, my original email, his approval reply, and the client message from Friday night. Then I forwarded everything to payroll and human resources with his new written demand attached. I did not accuse him of anything. I simply asked which policy allowed an employee's wages to be deducted for changes made by a manager after approval. Human resources replied twenty minutes later asking me not to sign anything and not to discuss deductions with my manager until they reviewed the records. By lunchtime, payroll confirmed that no deduction had been authorized. The next morning, my manager cancelled our team meeting and spent most of the day in a conference room with HR. The client had apparently complained not only about the incorrect pricing but also about being told that the analyst had caused the error. When HR compared the document history with the emails, the timeline was impossible to explain away. My manager tried to say he had only corrected formatting, but the archive showed every changed cell. He then claimed I had told him the new percentages verbally. That argument lasted until HR played the recording from our approved project call, where I had specifically warned him not to change the provisional figures until finance confirmed them. The company apologized to the client, restored the original pricing, and assigned another manager to the account. My deduction notice disappeared. A week later, HR asked me to attend a follow-up meeting. They told me the company had introduced a rule requiring a second approval for any manager who edited financial figures after an analyst signed off. They also reimbursed the overtime I had spent reconstructing the audit trail. My former manager was moved away from client pricing work and stopped speaking to me except through email. The funniest part came at the end of the month. Finance sent our team a reminder about document controls with an example showing exactly what not to do. The example was his Friday-night edit, with the names removed but every bad percentage still visible. He had tried to make me pay for his mistake, and somehow ended up becoming the company's training material instead.

youtube.description: My boss blamed me for his edit until the audit history told the whole story.
